title: Eliphaz Again: The Fate of the Wicked
summary: Eliphaz opens the second round of speeches, now far less gentle. He says Job's words are empty wind, that his own mouth condemns him, and that he is undermining the fear of God. Mocking Job's claim to wisdom, he asks whether Job was born before the hills or sat in God's council, then gives a long description of the wicked man who lives in terror and ends in ruin.
story: The first round of the debate is over. Each friend has spoken, and Job has answered each, ending in chapter 14 with a meditation on death and a flicker of hope beyond it. None of the friends has moved him, and Job has grown bolder, demanding a hearing with God and calling his friends worthless physicians (13:4). The second round begins here, and the tone hardens. In the first round the friends offered Job a way back: repent and be restored. In the second round (chapters 15 to 21) all three friends give almost no promise of restoration. Instead they describe, at length, the terrible fate of the wicked, leaving Job to draw the conclusion about himself.
historical:
Eliphaz is from Teman, a name associated with Edom, the land southeast of the Dead Sea. Teman was known for its wisdom: Jeremiah asks whether there is no longer wisdom in Teman (Jeremiah 49:7), and Obadiah speaks of the wise men of Edom (Obadiah 8). So the oldest and most respected of the friends comes from a region famous for its sages, which gives weight to his appeal to wise men and their fathers in verses 17-19.

Verse 19 describes those ancestors as people to whom alone the land was given, when no foreigner passed among them. Eliphaz means that the tradition he received is pure and unmixed, handed down in a people undisturbed by outsiders. The line reflects a common ancient belief that the oldest teaching was the most reliable. It does not point to a specific historical event that can now be identified.
cultural:
Eliphaz's mocking questions in verses 7-8 draw on ideas his hearers would recognize. Being born before the hills would make someone as old as the world itself; Proverbs 8:25 uses almost the same phrase of personified wisdom, brought forth before the hills. The council of God pictures God surrounded by heavenly beings who hear his plans, a scene found in 1 Kings 22:19-22 and Jeremiah 23:18 and already presented in Job 1 and 2. To claim access to that council was to claim prophetic knowledge. Eliphaz is saying Job speaks as though he were the first man or a member of God's cabinet.

The portrait of the wicked man in verses 20-35 uses familiar images. The hot east wind (verse 2) was the scorching wind from the desert, the sirocco, that withered crops. A face covered with fat (verse 27) pictured arrogant self-indulgence. A vine that drops its unripe grapes and an olive tree that sheds its blossoms (verse 33) both fail to bear fruit, and in an agricultural world that was a picture of a life that comes to nothing.
literary: Eliphaz's second speech has two parts of nearly equal weight. Verses 2-16 rebuke Job: his words are wind, his mouth condemns him, his claim to wisdom is arrogant, and he rejects the gentle consolations of God. Verses 14-16 repeat, almost as a formula, Eliphaz's earlier teaching (4:17-19) that no human can be pure before God. Verses 17-35 are an extended portrait of the wicked man, introduced as ancestral wisdom. It moves from inner terror (verses 20-24) to its cause, defiance of God (verses 25-26), and then to its end in ruin, fire, and barrenness (verses 27-35). The final image, conceiving trouble and giving birth to evil, is a proverbial picture of sin producing its own harvest (compare Psalm 7:14). Nothing in the portrait names Job, but everything in it is aimed at him.

outline.t: Were you born before the hills?
No human is pure before God
The ancestral portrait of the wicked man's end

doctrines.note: Eliphaz states a real biblical truth in verses 14-16: no human being is pure before a holy God. His mistake is to use this universal truth as though it explained Job's specific suffering.

The chapter's long portrait of the wicked describes God's judgment on those who defy him. The Bible affirms that judgment, but Job and later Psalm 73 both observe that it is not always visible within a lifetime.

Eliphaz asks whether Job has listened in on God's council. The question raises what the book will explore: human beings know God's purposes only as far as he reveals them, and the friends, like Job, have not seen what happened in heaven.

words.note: Sod, council or confidential counsel, the circle of those who share a leader's secrets. Used of God's council, it means the heavenly assembly where his purposes are spoken (Jeremiah 23:18, 22). Eliphaz's mocking question in verse 8 is ironic, since the reader has already seen God's council in chapters 1 and 2 and knows none of the speakers were there.

Tanchum, consolation or comfort. Eliphaz calls his own words the consolations of God (verse 11), treating the friends' speeches as God's comfort that Job is refusing. Job will answer in the next chapter by calling them miserable comforters.

Yirah, fear, especially the reverent fear of God that the wisdom books call the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Eliphaz charges Job with undermining it (verse 4), a serious accusation since Job was introduced as a man who feared God (1:1).

Chaneph, godless or profane, one who has turned away from God. Eliphaz uses it in verse 34 for the company of the godless. Job had used the same word in 13:16 to say no godless man can appear before God, and Eliphaz seems to turn it back on him.

christ: Eliphaz's sarcastic questions in verses 7-8 have an unexpected resonance in the New Testament. He mocks Job for acting as though he were born before the hills or had heard God's secret counsel. Proverbs 8:25 uses the same image of personified wisdom, present before the hills, and New Testament writers describe Christ in terms that echo that wisdom tradition: the firstborn over all creation, in whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15-17). John's Gospel says that no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is at the Father's side, has made him known (John 1:18). What Eliphaz treats as absurd for any human being, Christians confess of Christ. This is a thematic link, not a prediction, and Eliphaz means nothing of the kind. It shows the gap between human claims to wisdom and the wisdom God actually sends.

hard.q: Is Eliphaz's portrait of the wicked man true? Do the wicked always live in terror and die in ruin?
hard.a: Eliphaz describes a wicked man who writhes in pain all his days, lives with sounds of terror in his ears, and loses everything. Much of this matches what Scripture says elsewhere about the end of those who defy God, and Proverbs often speaks of the wicked coming to ruin. But Eliphaz presents it as an observable rule in this life, and that is where Job pushes back. In chapter 21 Job will answer that many wicked people live long, die in peace, and are buried with honor. Psalm 73 records the same troubled observation before its writer understands their final end. Many readers conclude that Eliphaz's portrait is true as a statement about God's final judgment but false as a description of how every life visibly turns out. The book of Job exists in large part to expose that difference, and Eliphaz's use of the portrait against Job is part of what God later rebukes (42:7).

questions: Eliphaz calls his own words the consolations of God. How can we tell whether the comfort we offer others really comes from God or only from our own assumptions?
Eliphaz appeals to the wisdom of the ancestors to silence Job. When is tradition a gift in hard times, and when can it become a weapon?
The friends in this round stop offering hope and only describe the fate of the wicked. Why do you think that happens in conflicts, and how can it be avoided?
